title: Post-Purchase Resolution
pitch: When a purchase goes wrong, WebMCP helps an agent find the right Shopify order and prepare a resolution—without taking authority away from the customer or merchant.
about_excerpt: When a purchase goes wrong, WebMCP helps an agent find the right Shopify order and prepare a resolution—without taking authority away from the customer or merchant. Like Comment Story Updates Post-Purchase Resolution Shopping agents know how to buy. What happens when something goes wrong? Post-Purchase Resolution is an agent-native post-purchase support experience built with WebMCP + Shopify . Instead of forcing a customer to search for an order number, navigate support menus, or explain the same problem several times, the customer can simply describe what went wrong in natural language. The agent can then discover the website's structured WebMCP capabilities, find the correct purchase, read authoritative Shopify state, and prepare the next step. But there is one deliberate boundary: The agent can help. It cannot silently become the customer or the merchant. The customer keeps customer authority. The merchant keeps merchant authority. Shopify remains the external source of truth. 🎥 Demo Watch the full demo In the demo, a customer reports that a Portable 4K Action Camera — $149 arrived damaged and would not turn on. The customer never provides an order number. From that natural-language request, the agent discovers the site's WebMCP tools, finds the correct authenticated purchase, reads its return eligibility, and prepares a resolution. Then: Agent prepares → Customer commits → Merchant decides → Shopify records the truth. 💡 Inspiration AI shopping experiences are becoming increasingly capable before checkout. Agents can search. They can compare. They can recommend. They can help people buy. But commerce does not end at checkout. Products arrive damaged. The wrong variant is delivered. Shipments arrive late. Customers need exchanges, returns, replacements, or refunds. And that part of the experience is still dominated by: order numbers support menus forms ticket queues policy pages repeated explanations disconnected customer and merchant workflows That led us to a simple question: If the web is becoming agentic, what should happen when the purchase itself goes wrong? We did not want to build another chatbot floating on top of an ecommerce site. We wanted the website itself to expose meaningful, structured capabilities that an agent could understand and use safely. That is where WebMCP became the core of the product rather than an add-on. ✨ What it does Post-Purchase Resolution lets a customer describe a purchase problem naturally. For example: “The action camera I bought recently arrived damaged and won't turn on. Can you find the purchase and tell me what I can do? Don't submit anything.” The customer does not need to know the order number. The agent discovers the site's available WebMCP tools and can use: find_order get_order prepare_resolution The experience then separates responsibility between three actors. 🤖 Agent The agent can: understand the customer's intent locate the relevant purchase read authoritative order information inspect return eligibility prepare the appropriate resolution The agent cannot commit the commerce action through WebMCP. 👤 Customer The authenticated customer decides whether to actually request the return. That action occurs under the customer's own Shopify Customer Account authority. 🏪 Merchant The merchant receives the pending request in a separate decision desk. Only the merchant can approve it. 🟢 Shopify Shopify records the authoritative lifecycle of the return. The website does not invent its own version of commerce state. 🔥 Why WebMCP matters Without structured site capabilities, an agent often has to reason from presentation: inspect UI interpret text locate controls infer what a button means navigate DOM state hope the page still looks the same Post-Purchase Resolution instead exposes explicit business capabilities. Customer intent ↓ ChatGPT / Codex ↓ WebMCP Site Tools ↓ find_order get_order prepare_resolution ↓ Authoritative Shopify data This means the agent does not need to guess that a certain button or piece of text represents an order lookup. The site tells the agent exactly what capability exists. And just as importantly, it tells the agent what capability does not exist. 🔐 The capability boundary This became one of the most important design decisions in the project. The WebMCP surface intentionally contains: ✓ find_order ✓ get_order ✓ prepare_resolution It intentionally does not contain: ✕ request_return ✕ approve_return ✕ refund That is not an unfinished feature. It is the authority model. The agent can find, read, and prepare. The customer commits. The merchant decides. This allowed us to design the experience around collaboration instead of maximum agent autonomy. More agent capability is not always better. The right capability at the right boundary is better. 🛍️ A real end-to-end scenario One of our clean validation runs used a fresh Shopify purchase that was never hardcoded into the application. The application discovered the purchase automatically. The customer then followed the complete flow. Fresh purchase ↓ Agent discovers purchase ↓ Agent prepares resolution ↓ Customer explicitly requests return ↓ Shopify Return = REQUESTED ↓ Merchant reviews request ↓ Merchant approves ↓ Same Shopify Return = OPEN The critical part is that the same external Shopify Return object is preserved throughout the lifecycle. The application is not maintaining a parallel pretend state. Shopify is the system of record. 🧪 Real Shopify proof We verified the architecture against a Shopify development store using test payments and real Shopify Order/Return objects . A clean flow demonstrated: Step Result Fresh order discovered without hardcoding ✅ Customer-scoped purchase ✅ Agent mutation tool exposed No Customer requested return ✅ Shopify Return created REQUESTED Merchant reviewed same Return ✅ Merchant approved ✅ Same Shopify Return updated OPEN Duplicate Return created No Refund automatically performed No This distinction matters. The agent did not manufacture a UI result. The state transition existed independently in Shopify. 🗣️ Natural-language WebMCP verification We also tested the WebMCP experience through ChatGPT/Codex Site Tools. The user described a damaged purchase without giving an order number. The agent discovered and used: find_order get_order prepare_resolution It found the correct purchase and prepared the resolution. Nothing was submitted. An independent Shopify check confirmed: Return created by agent: NO Refund created by agent: NO Approval event: NO We then repeated the experience using a spoken request in a new chat with no previous order context . The observed flow was: Spoken request ↓ ChatGPT agent turn ↓ Website Site Tools enumerated ↓ find_order ↓ get_order ↓ Correct purchase found The spoken request asked only to find the purchase and explain the available option.
